Good morning, Excellencies, distinguished participants. I declare open the first session of the Open-Ended Intergovernmental Working Group for the Elaboration of Legally Binding Instruments on the Promotion and Protection of the Human Rights of Older Persons. Our Working Group The Special Rapporteur on Older Persons, established by Human Rights Council Resolution 58/13, is mandated to elaborate and submit to the Human Rights Council a draft international legally binding instrument on the human rights of older persons with the objective of promoting, protecting, and ensuring the full enjoyment of human rights by older persons. I have the pleasure of welcoming the Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, Mrs. Awadabo, who is with us this morning to deliver opening remarks. Deputy High Commissioner, you have the floor.

Thank you, sir. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, good afternoon. It is an honor to join you today at the opening of the— of this first session of the Intergovernmental Working Group mandated to elaborate a legally binding instrument on human rights of older persons. This initiative comes at a decisive moment. Across the globe, a profound demographic transformation is underway. Population aging is no longer a trend confined to a few regions. By the late 2070s, the global population aged 65 and older is projected to surpass the number of children under the age of 18 worldwide. This structural shift will have far-reaching implications for our societies, for health and long-term care systems, for labor markets and pension systems, for family structures and care responsibilities, for humanitarian response, and centrally, for the daily enjoyment of human rights by older persons. Currently, ageism and discrimination, violence, neglect, and abuse, inadequate social protection, gaps in health and long-term care, and barriers to meaningful participation remain widespread. These are not isolated issues. They appear across very different legal, economic and cultural contexts, and they point to the same underlying problem: that older persons too often remain invisible in the interpretation, implementation, and enforcement of rights. This is precisely why a dedicated legal instrument on the human rights of older persons is needed. Older persons are already rights holders under the international law of human rights, international law of human rights, but the existing framework was not designed with the specific and cumulative forms of discrimination and exclusion that they experience. As a result, important protection often remains implicit, unevenly applied, or difficult to claim in practice. A legally binding instrument would change this. It would provide older persons and organizations that represent them a concrete legal basis on which to claim their rights, and give states a clear framework around which to build law and policy and services. It would also inform budgetary and programmatic choices, and provide a reference point across different national contexts. By establishing this Working Group, the Human Rights Council entrusted you with an ambitious mandate, bringing us closer than ever to ensuring that older persons are able to enjoy all of their human rights. Our Office stands ready to support this process. We look forward to walking this path together with Member States, civil society, and older persons' organizations in the months ahead. Thank you.

Firstly, on the contents, the instrument should be guided by a clear human rights-based framework that recognizes older persons as full rights holders entitled to the equal enjoyment of all human rights and fundamental freedoms on an equal basis with others and without discrimination, while also clarifying areas where further normative development is needed. It should move away from needs-based and medicalized approaches and instead affirm that the barriers faced by older persons stem from social, legal, environmental, economic, and institutional factors that limit the full enjoyment of rights and participation in society. It should also affirm the importance of full, meaningful, and effective participation of older persons and their representative organizations, including through consultation, co-design, and co-decision mechanisms. Secondly, on the structure, the Convention should adopt a clear, coherent, comprehensive framework consistent with the architecture of existing human rights treaties while remaining responsive to the specific protection gaps that continue to leave older persons insufficiently protected. A possible structure, fully detailed in our written submission, could include: 1, a preamble section recognizing ageism as a major cause of discrimination, exclusion, and denial of rights; 2, purpose, scope, and definitions, setting out the object and scope of the Convention, General principles and general obligations of the state parties. Thank you, Chair Rapporteur. We welcome the convening of this first session of the Intergovernmental Working Group and commend the Human Rights Council for establishing this important process through Resolution 58/13. This is a timely and necessary step towards addressing a long-standing nomadic gap in the international human rights system. Older persons are not passive recipients of care or charity. They are rights holders entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights and fundamental freedoms. Yet millions continue to face discrimination, abuse, neglect, exclusion, poverty, and barriers to justice simply because of their age. As we often say, a society reveals its true character not by how it treats its strongest members, but how it protects those most vulnerable. If rights diminish with age, then they were never truly rights at all. South Africa therefore strongly supports the elaboration of a comprehensive legally binding international instrument on the promotion and protection of human rights of older persons. We particularly welcome the Chair's food for thought paper which provides a useful and pragmatic basis for our discussions. Its emphasis on not binding from scratch— not building from scratch is very important. In our view, the instrument should build on existing international human rights law while responding directly to the realities of aging. It should include a clear preamble, definitions where necessary, general principles, substantive rights, implementation and monitoring provisions, and final clauses. Such an instrument must be grounded in dignity, equality, autonomy, participation, and non-discrimination, accessibility, accountability, and intergenerational solidarity. It must explicitly address ageism, and recognize that older persons are not a homogeneous group. The treaty should reflect the lived realities of older women, persons with disabilities, rural older persons, those in institutions, and those requiring support. South Africa further believes that the instrument should translate existing rights into concrete obligations for States. It should strengthen access to justice, recognize supported decision-making, and respect for will and preferences. And addresses care as a human rights issue and shared responsibility of families, communities, and the state. It will also give due attention to digital inclusion, health, long-term care, and protection from abuse, neglect, and exploitation. South Africa also supports the Roberts Implementation and monitoring arrangements, including periodic state reporting, independent oversight, and meaningful participation by older persons and civil society. This is an opportunity to ensure that advancing in age never means diminishing in rights. As member states, we should engage constructively and ambitiously so that we can deliver a strong, practical, and truly transformative legally binding instrument for present and future generations of older persons. I thank you.

And I encourage many other countries that have small delegations to participate actively in this process because it really helps us to see different perspectives. We don't want to have a perspective only from developing countries or from one area, from one region. We want the whole participation, not only NGOs but also from the side of the member states from all regions in the world, and the larger number of of regions and countries participating that will enrich even more and more this process that we just started. Thank you again, distinguished representative of Togo. Now, I give you the floor to distinguished representative of Slovenia. Slovenia has been one of the pillars, if not the pillar, of this process. Thank you, Mr. Chair. It is an honour to address you today. As you said, for more than a decade Slovenia has been advocating for stronger protection of the rights of older persons. And this session is a joyous occasion for us. Today we are starting to move from words to action, to setting standards. And we move from aspiration to obligation. Despite the universality of human rights, older persons too often remain invisible, within international legal frameworks. In times of swift demographic changes and an international framework that is uneven in the protection of human rights of older persons and at times blind to their specificities and vulnerabilities, Slovenia firmly believes these gaps and limitations in international human rights law must be comprehensively addressed. While existing treaties proclaim equality and non-discrimination, none contains comprehensive provision addressing ageism. A legally binding International Convention on the Rights of Older Persons will provide what is currently missing: a comprehensive framework of global standards. We need an instrument that will provide a strong legal framework to safeguard dignity, equality, and inclusion of older persons in practice, not just in principle. We see the new LBI as an integral part of the international human rights treaties, thus firmly grounded in human rights. As such, it can also offer a single platform for advocacy and a powerful instrument for accountability. Among general guiding principles, we prioritize non-discrimination, equality, including gender equality, respect for inherent dignity and autonomy, participation and inclusion in society, accessibility, and consistency with existing international human rights standards. The drafting process itself is a vehicle for constructive international dialogue and cooperation. Through it, we can share good practices, learn from diverse legal traditions, and build consensus around principles that reflect our common humanity. We can demonstrate that multilateralism remains capable of responding to emerging challenges with vision, conviction, and solidarity. It is essential that the process ensures active and meaningful participation of all relevant stakeholders, from member states to civil society, national human rights institutions, academia, and most importantly, it must be guided by the voices and lived experience of older persons themselves. They are not merely subjects of discussions, they are agents of change. Older persons from a significantly— form a significantly heterogeneous group. They are rights holders, yet too often perceived as merely social welfare beneficiaries. Mr. Chair, this process should build on the work of the existing and past mechanisms and processes, including the findings of the Open-Ended Working Group on Ageing and the Independent Expert, relevant reports of the Office of the High Commissioner, as well as regional efforts and legal frameworks. We will actively engage in the work of the Working Group, both at formal sessions and beyond. This Working Group offers us all an incredible opportunity to spearhead the transformation of the societal approach in understanding ageing and longevity. We thus invite you all to engage constructively in this endeavour. Thank you.

Thank you, distinguished representative of Slovenia, and I want to mentioned something that is extremely important. When we have the responsibility to mobilize energies and people and processes like this, it's not automatic. And normally there are people behind— not normally, always there are people behind. But there are some people who does more than others. And on this matter, specifically on this matter, many others as well, but in this matter, I want really to highlight the, uh, one of the major pillars in the person of the Ambassador Anita Pivan from Slovenia. She was always there pushing, really keeping this process alive. When everybody was discouraged, she was always there to make others to move on on this process. I mean, if it's someone in Geneva that really deserves all the honor for the reason that we are here today, I can tell you without a doubt that Ambassador Pipan is the person. We owe her a lot as international community. Thank you, Anita. Thank you for everything. Now I give the floor to distinguished representative of Malta. You have the floor.

Thank you, Chair Rapporteur, and I echo your Admiration for the work of Ambassador Pippin. Malta aligns itself with the EU statement. We welcome the first formal session of the Intergovernmental Working Group on Older Persons pursuant to the HRC Resolution 5813. At this working group, as it commences its work, the rights of older persons have reached an important milestone. As mandated by the HRC Resolution 5813, this working group will elaborate and submit to the HRC a draft binding instrument on the human rights of older persons. The Council also mandated that this future instrument would have as its main objective promotion, protection, and to ensure the full enjoyment of human rights of older persons. It is with these considerations in mind that Malta approaches the Working Group sessions. Elaborating a legally binding instrument is a laborious process, and we seek the Chair-Rapporteur's wisdom and patience to guide this process efficiently while at the same time ensuring its integrity. We recognize all States, in particular the members of the Core Group and civil society organizations that have worked tirelessly over several years for this process to reach this point. Malta is proud to have done its part in 1969 at the UN General Assembly, when it raised what at the time was termed protection of the rights and assured the welfare of the aged in Article 11 of the Declaration on Social Progress and Development of 1969. Mr. Chair Rapporteur, the terminology we use at the UN today may have changed and become more inclusive, but our aim remains the same: that of ensuring that older persons have and continue to have their rights protected in full, without any form of discrimination. We see this as a major priority for this Working Group. Mr. Chair Rapporteur, the documents prepared by the Secretariat for this session are important because they set out the general guiding principles of this process. We thank the Secretariat for their work. While we do encourage earlier distribution of documentation for future sessions, to provide enough time for in-depth preparation by delegations. Mr. Chair-Rapporteur, we thank you for circulating the Food for Thought paper, about which we will make more detailed comments under the relevant agenda item. Malta had also submitted a contribution, which is reflected on the IJWG website, in preparation to this process, which also includes various elements which we deem as highly relevant for the eventual legally binding instrument. In our view, drafting such an important instrument not only should include more traditional aspects related to the rights of older persons, but also be able to reflect contemporary challenges perhaps not fully envisaged in earlier years. We consider it expedient that through this process, an eventual instrument will be relevant then as it would be now. We look forward to engaging during this process to formulate a legally binding instrument And through our collective efforts, we hope that in the final determination, older persons' rights will be better protected as rights holders. I thank you.
Thank you, distinguished representative of Malta. Thank you for your contributions. And I give the floor to distinguished representative of the Russian Federation. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. First of all, we would like to express our appreciation for convening this first session. Which marks the beginning of a long way ahead of intense work and thorough negotiations. We appreciate the opportunity to express our preliminary views and opinions on this important initiative and to underline our sincere commitment to engage constructively to this upcoming process. We strongly believe that the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities could be a good basis and start or guidance for us to start elaborating the text, given the fact that the thematic spheres of both documents are quite close and that the CRPD is the most recent— recently adopted universal document on human rights. The Russian Federation will also be sharing its own best practices and achievements, including those which are contained in our national strategy on this matter. With regard to the core principles of the future Convention, we believe they could be the concepts enshrined in CRPD: respect for the dignity of older persons, their personal autonomy and independence, prohibition of discrimination based on age, full and effective participation and inclusion in society, respect for the distinctiveness of older persons, equal opportunity, accessibility, equality between men and women. Furthermore, additional principles could be drawn from the Charter of Older Persons adopted by Resolution No. 1115 of the Interparliamentary Assembly of the Commonwealth of Independent States in 1998, ensuring a dignified experience, security, and the practical possibility of realizing the full human potential of older persons. Persons, and the 2015 Inter-American Convention on the Rights of Older Persons, which recognized the important role of older persons in society, their self-realization, the principles of solidarity, protection of the family, the responsibility of the state, and the participation of family and society in realizing the rights of older persons. With regard to the structure of the future international treaty, we believe that it would consist of the following elements. Preamble, articles concerning the general provisions such as purpose, definitions, general principles, general obligations, articles disclosing the content of key principles, the content of individual rights, both universal and specific, as well as articles on international cooperation, on implementation at the national level, on conventional mechanisms, a conference of state parties to the international treaty or a potential Committee on the Rights of Older Persons, as well as final clauses. With regard to the substantive content of the document, in addition to the provisions that could be found in the CRPD, we also would like to suggest a few— to make a few suggestions with regard to include or to cover possible rights which could be enshrined in these legally binding documents. Among them, a right to have a guaranteed pension, specific special benefits and other sources of incomes, to receive reliable protection for their savings and incomes, to freely choose their place of residence. During this session, we'll be presenting more inputs for this text, and for the sake of time, just keep it for later discussion. Thank you so much.

Thank you, distinguished representative of the Russian Federation. Thank you for your suggestions and and the contributions for this process. I give you the floor, distinguished representative of Jamaica. You have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. The Jamaican delegation welcomes this opportunity to participate in this first substantive session of the IGWG mandated to elaborate a legally binding international instrument for the promotion and protection of the human rights of older persons. This responds to a longstanding global recognition of gaps in the protection regime for older persons and builds upon years of work under the Madrid International Plan of Action on Aging. Our delegation approaches this process guided by our 2021 National Policy for Senior Citizens, which places strong emphasis on rights, responsibilities, and recognition of older persons' capabilities and contributions. We therefore affirm that the work of this IGWG must center on a comprehensive rights-based approach, ensuring that older persons are protected from discrimination, abuse, exploitation, and neglect, while being empowered to contribute to sustainable development. As Madam Deputy High Commissioner indicated, there is a profound demographic transition underway that is not confined to any particular region. Jamaica is experiencing this rapid demographic shift. Older persons now represent nearly 14% of our population, and this figure is expected to reach closer to 20% by 2030. This demographic transformation demands a global response that strengthens health systems, long-term care, and social protection to ensure older persons can live dignified, independent, and secure lives. With a steady increase in life expectancy and recognizing the vulnerabilities linked to aging, targeted evidence-based and rights-driven interventions would be required. For our part, Jamaica is currently taking steps to enact a comprehensive legislative framework for the care and protection of older persons, which aims to strengthen safeguards and protect the rights of older persons. Regarding principles at CHEAR, Jamaica's position is that the legally binding instrument should be guided by the principles of non-discrimination by age, participation and inclusion, Independence and autonomy, protection from all forms of abuse, violence, and exploitation, access to care, access to justice, and intergenerational solidarity. Regarding structure, we see the instrument being broadly framed by the following sections: a preamble, a statement of principles including those previously mentioned, general human rights obligations for States reflecting a reiteration of the rights to be enjoyed by older persons, monitoring and implementation, as well as final provisions. In closing, Chair, Jamaica stands ready to work with all delegations to ensure that we produce an instrument that meaningfully advances the dignity, rights, and well-being of older persons everywhere. We owe it to current and future generations to ensure that aging is not treated as a vulnerability or burden, but as an integral, respected, and supported phase of life. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you, distinguished representative of Jamaica. Thank you for your contributions, for your suggestions, and the support to this process. And now I give the floor to distinguished representative of Iran. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Chair Rapporteur, Iran welcomes the convening of the first session of the Intergovernmental Working Group. At the outset, we wish to stress that in many cultures, especially in Eastern societies, older persons are respected members of society. They pass on knowledge, wisdom, and experience. Experience from one generation to another. They play an important role in families and communities. Therefore, any future instruments should be based on respect for their dignity and contribution to society. We also reaffirm the value of every human life and reject any approach that weakens the protection of life and the dignity of older persons. Mr. Chair, as we discuss the rights of older persons, we should also recognize the different situations faced by developing countries. Many of these countries have a large younger population that needs jobs, housing, and education, while at the same time they must respond to the growing needs of older persons. With limited national resources, the challenges cannot be addressed without stronger international cooperation. In this regard, we wish to highlight the harmful effects of UCMs, including economic and financial sanctions. Such measures undermine the right to development of affected countries, weaken their health system, and limit their ability to provide adequate health and care services for older persons. They also restrict access to essential medicines, medical equipment, assistive devices, supportive technologies, and other basic goods needed by older persons. As a result, they directly affect the health, dignity, and quality of life of older persons. The future instrument should therefore recognize not only the obligation of states to protect the rights of older persons within their own countries, but also their obligation to refrain from action that harms the rights of older persons in other countries. States should ensure that their policies and measures do not hinder the enjoyment of human rights in either other countries. Mr. Chair, finally, we remain committed to working with all delegations to develop a balanced, practical, and effective instrument that effectively protects the rights and dignity of older persons. Thank you.
Thank you, distinguished representative of Iran. Thank you for your statement. And I give the floor to distinguished representative of the Philippines. You have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. The Philippines reaffirms its support to the mandate of this working group. Population aging is an inescapable global reality. A legally binding instrument codifying the rights of older persons and the corresponding obligations of duty bearers will provide a holistic and rights-based framework to respond to the challenges and opportunities presented by this demographic transition. The Philippines envisions an instrument that unequivocally recognizes older persons as rights holders, not merely recipients of care or charity from the state and society. Its objective should be to empower older persons everywhere so they can live in in autonomy, dignity, and full participation in society. By reaffirming this agency, the instrument will reinforce a fundamental truth that human rights are universal, inalienable, and must be enjoyed all throughout the life cycle. The principle of non-discrimination and intergenerational solidarity should underpin the LBI. They should be complemented by protection and procedural rights and guarantees, including access to affordable, humane, and dignified long-term care and palliative services. In this regard, this— the indispensable role of caregivers must be recognized. The rights of caregivers Particularly migrant caregivers, must also be protected so that they can provide the highest standard of care while preserving their own dignity and well-being. Finally, the Philippines underscores the importance of an inclusive process where civil society, national human rights institutions, and other stakeholders participate meaningfully while upholding the intergovernmental nature of the negotiations. The Philippines will work constructively with all delegations and stakeholders to deliver a robust, effective, and forward-looking instrument for the world of today and of future generations. Thank you.
Thank you, distinguished representatives of the Philippines. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Colombia. Muchas gracias.

Thank you, Chairperson. Congratulations on your election. We support this intergovernmental work. Group and the need for an international legally binding instrument on the rights of older persons. We welcome this first negotiating session. The international instrument must be based on general principles of international human rights law, including human dignity, universality, equality, and non-discrimination, indivisibility and interdependence of human rights. It is crucial to incorporate progressiveness and non-regression, encouraging states to expand the rights of older persons. These principles must make it possible expressly to address ageism, which is a form of structural discrimination aggravated when it also involves ethnic origin, gender, or disability. The 5 pillars of the United Nations on the basis of— for older persons: independence, participation, care, self-realization, dignity overlap with co-responsibility of the state, the family, and the community. The development of regional systems such as the Inter-American System for Older Persons adapted by our country in 2000 2022 could be useful. We also believe it is essential to incorporate accessibility and reasonable accommodations guaranteeing access to physical environments, technology, and services overcoming barriers to full participation. The instrument must recognize the legal capacity of older persons on equal footing and their right to decide for themselves. We note the relevance of making care a human right with co-responsibility and recognition of unpaid care incorporating progressive deinstitutionalization of community-based care. Thank you. In conclusion, we reiterate our readiness actively and constructively to participate in negotiations, trusting that this will lead to progress on a solid, comprehensive, transformative instrument that meets the current needs and ensures that all older persons may fully exercise their rights in autonomy and free from all forms of discrimination. I thank you.

Muchas gracias. I thank Colombia and I have to mention that 2 weeks ago we also still had inside this process our colleague Ambassador Gayon who left us so suddenly. And I want to draw everybody's attention to the fact that this process is one that is to transform lives when we seek to transform the lives of millions of people. It is important to take into account urgency, the urgency of this process, and at the same time make sure it is solid and has sound foundations. At the same time, we have to address the need for Rapid solutions, and this is my tribute to our excellent colleague. We are all aware of the need to work together hand in hand in order to ensure that this process may be achieved as. soon as possible. We thank you. With that, I thank you and I give the floor to Indonesian.

Mr. Chair, we wish to join others to congratulate you on your appointment as chair reporter of this working group. We count on your leadership in guiding this working group's deliberations in accordance with Human Rights Council Resolution 58/13. Indonesia recognizes older persons as right holders, defined by our national law as those aged 60 years and above. Their rights on equal basis with all other Indonesian citizens are legally protected, including inter alia their access to healthcare, employment, education, and social protection. Ensuring older persons' welfare is our development priority, which is increasingly urgent as we are entering an aging society. Indonesia is now home to nearly 35 million older persons, projected to reach 65 million by 2045. In response to this demographic transition, we are in the process of amending our law on older persons' welfare, reflecting our sustained and adaptive measure to further advance their fundamental rights. For us, their wisdom, knowledge, and experience continue to foster our families, communities, and national resilience and remain an important source of guidance for all present and future generations. Mr. Chair, Indonesia believes that the elaborations of a draft LBI on older persons should not be pursued as a merely symbolic exercise but must serve these 3 main principles. First, it must genuinely address real normative gaps in international human rights law, grounded in empirical needs and the lived experience of older persons. Second, it must avoid unnecessary duplications of established principles and provisions applicable to all persons under existing international human rights instruments. Third, it must be consensus-oriented, anchored in universal human rights while taking due account of national circumstances, legal systems, cultural contexts, and local specificities. We also underline the need to carefully consider the practical implications of any future implementation and monitoring arrangement of the LBI. Creating undue additional burdens for states must be avoided, particularly amidst the ongoing UN liquidity constraints and reform efforts. Any proposal for a separate reporting mechanism should be carefully assessed, including the possibility of utilizing the existing treaty body mechanism. Mr. Chair, applying a balanced and consensual approach in this process is crucial to ensure a broad ownership and avoid polarization among member states. Indonesia's commitment to advancing the rights of older persons is firm, and we stand ready to engage in good faith in the work of this council— of this working group. I thank you.
Thank you. Thank you, distinguished representative of Indonesia. And I give the floor to distinguished representative of Thailand. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thailand joins you and other colleagues in expressing our appreciation to Ambassador Anita Papan of Slovenia for her leadership in this process and welcomes the convening of the first session of the Intergovernmental Working Group on the Human Rights of Older Persons. Thailand advocates for a human rights-based approach as the overarching framework with regard to the structure and guiding principles of the future international legally binding instrument. We view that this framework should adopt a similar approach taking in the development of the CRPD, it must shift the paradigm by transforming the status of older persons from mere recipients of welfare and protection to empower them as rights holders. To ensure consistency and reduce duplication, Thailand views that the structure of this new instrument must align with relevant existing frameworks Particularly the Madrid International Plan of Action on Aging, the Sustainable Development Goals, and the UN Decade of Healthy Aging. Regarding the core principles of the future instrument, Thailand believes that the following elements should be central to our deliberations. First, holding human dignity, autonomy, self-reliance, and equality alongside efforts to reduce ageism. Second, ensuring comprehensive income security for an adequate standard of living and promoting preparation for the pre-aging population. Third, guaranteeing the right of older persons to live with their families, communities, and societies by supporting community-based care, promoting aging in place, and ensuring caregivers' rights and protections. Fourth, securing the right of age-friendly primary care, prevention— preventive health screenings, long-term care, and palliative care. Fifth, protecting older persons during humanitarian situations, disasters, and emergencies. Sixth, fostering the right to participation, lifelong learning, and digital literacy. And 7, ensuring the right to adequate housing and supportive environments through the concept of universal design. Mr. Chair, we share your view that this cannot be achieved by one country alone. Thailand remains steadfast in our commitment to working constructively with all members and stakeholders to ensure the full and equal realization of human rights for all the persons. Thank you.
Thank you, distinguished representative of Thailand. I give the floor to distinguished representative of Iraq. You have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. Iraq wishes to express its appreciation for the efforts to hold this first session of the Open-Ended Working Group on Older Persons in line with Resolution 58/13. We took note of the results and recommendations of the Working Group on Aging and relevant reports, as well as participation of countries, relevant stakeholders, and the President's paper on enriching the debate. We hope all these efforts will enrich the discussions, given that the paper includes consensual elements in line with the program of work. Chair Iraq is fully aware of the importance of the working group's discussions, given that human rights treaties do not cover issues of older persons directly, and we see also an increase in the number of aging and an increase. In normative gaps and protection. We call for also drafting that complement gaps in existing treaties and while focusing on the right to difference in national capacities and reinforcing international cooperation and exchange of expertise while taking into account specificities of countries, while supporting the family at the cornerstone for the protection of the rights of older persons and their dignity. This meeting should focus on agreeing to a clear work methodology and a framework in order to better use time and resources and prepare well to good and organized negotiations in order to achieve tangible progress away from repeating discussions and cumbersome procedures. We should use a constructive, consensual language and refrain from controversial, controversial languages in order to reach a text that reinforces our common goal, which is to provide sustainable protection for older persons. In closing, we forward to work with all delegations within a spirit of partnership in line with the agreed-upon program of work. And thank you, Chairperson.

Thank you, distinguished representative of Iraq. If you could please send in advance the, uh, your statements to the interpreters to speeches@un.org. That will help a lot for the benefit of everybody so that your statement will be clearly translated. And the other thing is that I haven't received any complaint by the interpreters yet, but I mean, if you could please slow down the statements, that could be really wonderful as well. Please. Thank you. Now I give the floor to distinguished representative of Uruguay.

Thank you, Chairperson. Uruguay reiterates its support for the negotiation of this international legally binding instrument on the human rights of older persons and welcomes the work done over the 2 decades. We seek inclusive participation in this process with significant participation by older persons in their full diversity throughout the process and participation by young people. We seek structural transformation based on international human rights law with the development of a universal instrument. This is a milestone in strengthening the protection of older persons, overcoming legislative gaps and providing clarity and guidance to states in their obligations. This instrument must be based on the premise that older persons enjoy all human rights and fundamental freedoms on an equal footing with others. Age does not justify restrictions on the enjoyment of rights. Uruguay believes that dignity and autonomy must be the axis of this future instrument. Personal autonomy, equality before the law, the right to take decisions on one's own life, full participation in society, access to adequate support, and the right to a life free of violence, discrimination, and abuse. The instrument must address current and emerging challenges that particularly address— face older persons, including armed conflict, digital transformation, digital gap, and climate change. It is crucial to incorporate the gender perspective and an intersectional approach, noting that older persons are not a homogeneous group. And that many of them face intersecting forms of discrimination, particularly older women, older persons with disabilities, Afro-descendant persons, indigenous persons, persons living in poverty, and persons in institutions. The future instrument must complement existing human rights treaties, overcoming gaps. Complementing the Inter-American Convention on the Rights of Older Persons, which is a valuable basis for development of international standards. We reiterate our commitment to constructively building this instrument to ensure that it is solid, universal, and based on dignity, autonomy, and equality for all older persons. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Uruguay. Thank you for your valuable contributions to this process. May you have a long—

Thank you, Mr. Chair. The translation didn't come through. And congratulations on your guiding voices. It's a pleasure to work under you. Germany aligns herself with the statement given by the European Union. In our national capacity, we also would like to thank the organizers for convening this crucial meeting to begin the substantial work of drafting a legally binding instrument on the promotion and protection of the human rights of older persons. Germany assures you to work constructively towards achieving this new instrument, and we welcome very much the active participation of the numerous civil society organizations we see in the room, the national human rights institutions, and the representatives of older persons. Germany has stated its opinion on the structure and guiding principles in answering the question sent out by OHCHR to prepare this session. As for guiding principles, I'd like to point out that the universality of human rights is the main principle that must prevail. The standards and norms included in the new legally binding instrument should be derived from the International Rights Archive and develop this Rights Archive. Thank you. Human rights have no age limit. Where specific rights already exist in the Human Rights Archive, the exact texts of existing rights have to be taken to a new legally binding instrument in order to avoid contradiction and confusion regarding the content and interpretation of rights by treaty bodies. No existing norm may be weakened. That includes the Human Rights Archive as well as the ILO standards for for social and labor rights, which complement the human rights acquis as universally agreed standards. This has been pointed out in our organizational meeting in February. The principle of intergenerational fairness should be incorporated into the new binding instrument as a guiding principle. As concluded by the Open-Ended Working Group on Aging, the principle of non-discrimination is especially the explicit ban on age discrimination and ageism in the field of human rights, must be the core principle of the new legally binding instrument. We think that CRPD must be a central guiding framework. A new legally binding instrument may not fall behind the widely agreed standards of this core international convention, which is the youngest internationally binding instrument. The structure should follow the standards of preamble recalling and reaffirming all existing treaties, scope definitions, general principles, and we think we should be very creative on a monitoring instrument. We need— think monitoring is essential, but we have to be creative to invent a mechanism which does not overburden the UN system and the parties to the new instrument. I would also like to draw your attention to the MIPoB process, which gives us underlying language. Germany will host the next UNECE Ministerial Conference, and we think that the negotiations in this room will be reflected in the conference. And furthermore, I would join the voices pleading for an earlier distribution of the papers to be better prepared for these meetings. Thank you so much.
Thank you, distinguished representative of Germany. The same response that I gave to the Austrian. I give the floor to distinguished representative of Dominican Republic. You have the floor.

Thank you, Chairperson. Dominican Republic welcomes the holding of the first session of the Working Group and congratulates you on your election. Our country participates as a member of the Group of Friends and the co-sponsor of the resolution that was at the basis of this process, noting that aging is one of the major contemporary challenges. The future convention must be based on clear principles for interpretation and implementation, including inherent dignity of the person, autonomy, independence, equality, and non-discrimination on the basis of age, full effective participation in society, accessibility, intergenerational solidarity, and recognition of the diversity of older persons. We support a structure which, without starting from zero, draws on the experience of other human rights treaties, incorporating the provisions that have shown themselves to be effective to ensure the protection of vulnerable groups while responding to specific challenges facing older persons. My country considers it crucial for the future instrument to have follow-up mechanisms that are effective, interdependent, and accessible, promote effective dialogue with states, and facilitate the exchange of good practice. Our commitment to this agenda has historic roots. The International Day of Older Persons on 1st of October internationally was an initiative of my country within the United Nations. Reflecting our sustained commitment to dignity and the rights of older persons. Internationally, we have strengthened the public policies for older persons through the work of the National Council for Aging Persons, the implementation of social protection programs, and the protection of active aging. My country therefore reiterates its readiness constructively to participate in flexible fashion seeking consensus within this process. I thank you.
I thank the Dominican Republic. Representative of Nigeria.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Nigeria reaffirms its support for the working group and reassures you of our continued cooperation as we begin this first substantive session. My delegation welcomes the opportunity to begin this important process and believe we all— we already have a good foundation regardless of the different Yes. While there may be differences between views on the form of future instrument it may take, or indeed whether one is required, there is broad recognition that other persons are entitled to the full enjoyment of their human rights and fundamental freedom. The task before us, therefore, is to ensure that our discussions remain practical and focused on finding solutions that will make a real difference in the lived realities of older persons. For Nigeria, this discussion extends beyond law and policy. It is also a development issue. As people live longer and our societies continue to evolve, it becomes imperative to strengthen healthcare, social protection, long-term care, and other support systems that enable older persons to live in dignity, independence, and security. In this regard, we believe any future instrument should recognize that in many societies, particularly in Africa, the family remains the primary and natural source of care and support for older persons. It should therefore strengthen the role of families, encourage community-based support, and implement and complement the efforts already being made by states. Nigeria also considers it important that this process builds on existing international human rights law while carefully addressing any identified gaps in a manner that commands the broadest consensus among member states. Finally, Nigeria looks forward to engaging constructively throughout this process in a spirit of dialogue, cooperation, and consensus with a view to developing an instrument that is practical, implementable, and responsive to the realities and needs of the old persons. I thank you.

Thank you, distinguished representative of Nigeria. Now I give the floor to distinguished representative of Namibia. Yeah, that's right. Representative of Namibia? Probably he's not in the room. I give you the floor to distinguished representative of United Arab Emirates. You have the floor.

Chair, we welcome the launch of the work of the Working Group on the Rights of Older Persons, which is going to develop an instrument on the rights of older persons. We congratulate you, Chairperson, for assuming the chairmanship of the Working Group. We are committed to the rights of older persons and their empowerment. This instrument is important for reinforcing international cooperation and developing a legal framework that keeps abreast with demographic transformations and meets the needs of societies in a comprehensive manner. The instrument should be based on the UN Charter, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the relevant instruments. While focusing on the UN principles on older persons and Madrid International Aging Work Plan, while taking into account different legal systems of various countries. For my country, protection of older persons is not merely a theoretical concept. It constitutes a national obligation deeply rooted in our constitution and our civilizational values. Our experience is backed by pioneering legislative framework which established We established a protective model based on the triptych of national, family, and intergenerational solidarity. Our legislation makes maintaining older persons within their family environment a cardinal principle and firmly criminalizes abandonment and abuse while guaranteeing baseline of economic resources and free healthcare. Mr. President, regarding the guiding principles, Algeria insists that any future treaty must not deal with the issue of older persons in isolation. The text must imperatively recognize the central role of the family as a fundamental unit of protection and social cohesion. However, to be fully effective, the general framework of this future instrument must demonstrate flexibility. It must be able to realistically adapt to national specificities, including different levels of socioeconomic development, institutional capacities, and the legitimate resource constraints of each country. In this regard, my delegation wishes to express certain concern regarding the potential duplication with existing international treaties, which already provide universal protection for human rights. We must ensure that we do not unduly increase the reporting burden that already weighs heavily on the administrations of developing countries. Furthermore, we call for caution against the risk of concept expansion, which could jeopardize the consensus and is possible for the universal ratification of this text. This is why we reaffirm that a holistic structure must place economic and social rights on an equal footing with civil and political rights. While relying on the principles of progressive realization and international cooperation. Developing countries must be supported through technical assistance in the respect of their national sovereignty. Algeria will continue to engage constructively in this debate to build a consensual and implementable institution— instrument. Thank you.
Thank you, distinguished representative of Kenya— excuse me, of Algeria. I'm going to give you the floor to distinguished representative of the State of Palestine. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair-Rapporteur. The State of Palestine congratulates you on your appointment and assures you of our full support in carrying out your mandate. We thank you for your efforts in guiding this important process and for the food for thought paper prepared to facilitate our discussions. We welcome this first session. The State of Palestine believes that the structure and guiding principles of the future legally binding instrument must reflect its center purpose, to ensure the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights by older persons and address the specific protection gaps they face. The instrument should, should be grounded in human dignity, equality, and non-discrimination, autonomy and independence, participation, inclusion, and accessibility. It must recognize older persons as full rights holders and active agents and ensure their meaningful participation and that of their representative organizations throughout its elaboration, implementation, and monitoring. It must also recognize that age does not operate in isolation. Intersectional, multiple, and cumulative discrimination should therefore be addressed across this instrument, as age may intersect with disability, sex, displacement, and other circumstances, creating distinct barriers to the enjoyment of rights. For the State of Palestine, The lived reality of older Palestinians demonstrates why these principles must be reflected throughout the instrument. Under prolonged foreign occupation and amidst Israel's ongoing genocide, older persons face repeated forced displacement, starvation, denial of medical care, and the destruction of essential, essential systems of support. Age compounds these violations, particularly for persons with disabilities or reduced mobility, Thank you, Mr. Chair. Mr. Chair, Rapporteur, international human rights law and international humanitarian law continue to apply and provide essential protections to the older persons in all circumstances. Yet the existing framework remains fragmented and does not comprehensively articulate the specific age-responsive measures required to ensure the full and equal enjoyment of these rights. The future instrument must therefore build upon and reinforce existing international law without diminishing existing protections. It must articulate clear age-responsive obligations applicable in all circumstances, including situations of risk, armed conflict, foreign occupation, and forced displacement. Its structure must be comprehensive, bringing together clear principles and General obligations, substantive rights, and effective provisions on implementation, monitoring, accountability, and remedies. The State of Palestine stands ready to engage constructively towards an instrument that places older persons at the center of this architecture. Thank you.
Thank you, distinguished representative of the State of Palestine. Thank you for your contribution. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Turkey.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Türkiye welcomes this opportunity to contribute to the discussion on the structure and guiding principles of a legally binding instrument on the human rights of older persons. Turkey considers that the future legally binding instrument must reaffirm that older persons are entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights and fundamental freedoms. Building upon the existing international human rights framework, it should provide greater clarity on the application of universally recognized human rights in the context of aging, thereby strengthening their effective implementation, and addressing the persistent protection and implementation gaps that older persons continue to face. Its added value should therefore lie in reinforcing the realization of existing human rights through enhanced legal clarity and implementation, rather than the creation of new rights. In this regard, Türkiye believes that the future instrument must recognize older persons as autonomous right stakeholders. Human dignity is to serve— I'm sorry. Human dignity is to serve as the overarching principle of the instrument, while equality and non-discrimination should constitute its core foundation. The instrument also needs to reflect a life course approach, recognizing the cumulative impact of inequalities throughout life and promoting active and healthy ageing. Particular importance should also be attached to the role of families, communities and intergenerational solidarity. While fully respecting the autonomy and preferences of older persons, the instrument should promote supportive environments that foster inclusion, social cohesion and community-based support. With regard to its structure, we consider that a clear and coherent architecture will be instrumental in ensuring the effectiveness of the instrument. A framework comprising a preamble, definitions, general principles, general obligations, substantive provisions, and implementation and monitoring mechanisms would provide a sound basis for both interpretation and implementation. Finally, while establishing common international standards, the instrument needs to retain sufficient flexibility to allow implementation in accordance with different national legal systems and national circumstances. Mr. Chair, Turkey stands ready to engage constructively and in the spirit of partnership as we move forward. I thank you.
